verses.translation_literal: A song of the ascents. From the depths I call to you, YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song for the climb. From the deep places, from the bottom of everything, I cry out to you, O LORD.
verses.directors_commentary: The title marks this as one of the fifteen Songs of the Ascents (Pss 120–134), sung by pilgrims climbing to Jerusalem; the KJV's "degrees" is the old word for steps. Play the opening against that title: the song is about going up, and it begins at the very bottom. "The depths" is a plural of intensity: the ancient world pictured the sea's floor and the waters of chaos as the place from which no one comes back (compare Ps 69:15, Jonah 2:3-6). Radak says the exile is pictured as the depths of the sea; Malbim adds that the depth can be inward as well as outward, a soul sunk low by its own sin. The verb is a perfect, which the KJV takes as a past ("have I cried"); it can also be read as a performative perfect, the cry made in the very act of speaking, "I call to you", which is how the literal layer renders it. Both readings are grammatical, so play it as a cry that is happening as the verse is spoken. The KJV also renders the divine name YHWH as "Lord", as most English versions do; the Hebrew has the personal name of Israel's God here, not a title.

philological_notes.note: A plural of intensity: not one deep place but the deepest of depths. The word is used elsewhere for deep waters (Ps 69:15; Isa 51:10), so the sea-floor image stands behind the abstract sense of distress. Radak reads it as the exile compared to the depths of the sea; Malbim reads it as both bodily lowness and a soul sunk by sin.

"The ascents", a plural of the same root as "go up". The title is shared by Pss 120–134; the usual explanation is the pilgrim's climb to Jerusalem, though the Targum here takes it as a song said over the steps of the abyss.

verses.translation_literal: My Lord, hear my voice; let your ears be attentive to the voice of my supplications.
verses.translation_dramatic: Lord, hear me. Hear my voice. Let your ears turn toward it and stay turned, toward the sound of my pleading.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker has called; now the voice asks to be heard. This is the language of a petitioner before a king: a plea has to reach the ear of the one who can act, and that ear is pictured as turned or inclined toward the speaker. The Hebrew does not say "my prayer" but "my voice" and "the voice of my supplications", twice: the cry is physical, a sound rising out of the depths. The Hebrew "ears" is a dual, both ears, and the KJV's "ears" keeps it, so the KJV is accurate in this verse: both ears, wholly given to the plea. The word for "supplications", from the root "to be gracious", is the voice of someone asking for favor he cannot claim. Note that the Lord is now addressed as אֲדֹנָי, "my Lord", the lord and master, where verse 1 used the divine name; the speaker moves from the name to the title of a servant before his master.

philological_notes.note: "Attentive", a rare adjective of the root meaning "to pay attention". Radak and Meiri observe that it is formed like שְׁכוֹלוֹת, a plural feminine adjective, agreeing with "ears". Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as a term for hearing.
"My supplications", from the root "to show favor": a plea for grace, not a claim of right.

verses.translation_literal: If iniquities you keep, O Yah, my Lord, who will stand?
verses.translation_dramatic: If you kept the record of our wrongs, O Yah, O Lord — who could stand?
verses.directors_commentary: The question is rhetorical and it is the pivot of the psalm: the speaker does not defend himself, he says that no one could. "Keep" (שׁמר) is the word for guarding, storing, holding something in reserve. The picture is of a ledger or a stored account, a debt kept on record until it is called in, and Metzudat David reads it as exactly this, punishment held in store. The KJV's "mark" is a fair guess but softens that: God does not merely notice sins, he could keep them. The KJV's "Lord... O Lord" hides that these are two different words: יָהּ is the short form of the divine name and אֲדֹנָי is the title. They are stacked together, a breath of the name and then "my Lord", as though the speaker cannot get the form of address right. "Stand" means to hold one's ground before a judge: the one who cannot stand falls, loses the case. Actors should not play the verse as a threat; it is a statement of fact said quietly, from the depths.

philological_notes.note: "You keep": guard, store up, retain. With "iniquities" it means to keep them on record rather than let them go. Meiri takes the conditional as: if you did not forgive upon repentance. The verb is the same root as "watchmen" in v. 6, a link between the two halves of the psalm.
"Iniquities": the word covers the wrong, its guilt and its consequence at once, which is why v. 8 can speak of being redeemed "from" them.

verses.translation_literal: For with you is the forgiveness, so that you may be feared.
verses.translation_dramatic: But with you there is forgiveness — and that is why you are feared.
verses.directors_commentary: The turn. "For" gives the reason that makes verse 3 bearable: the answer to "who can stand?" is that forgiveness is found with God, and nowhere else. The Hebrew says "the forgiveness", with the article, as if it were a known thing kept in one place. The word for forgiveness (סליחה) is used in Scripture only of God (here, Neh 9:17, Dan 9:9), a point Malbim presses: no passage of the Bible has one person "forgiving" another in this sense. The ending is the hard part for modern ears. The KJV's "that thou mayest be feared" is correct, but the reader hears fear as dread. Ibn Ezra and Malbim both explain it the other way: God forgives, and sinners, seeing it, turn back in awe; if there were no forgiveness, people would give up and do as they like. Fear here means reverence, the response of someone who has received what he could not claim. Rashi and Metzudat David add a second reading from Exodus 23:21 ("he will not pardon your transgression", said of the angel): God did not hand forgiveness to any messenger, so no one can count on a go-between's pardon.

philological_notes.note: "The forgiveness" with the article. The root is used in the Bible only with God as the subject. Malbim draws the conclusion that the source of pardon lies in God himself, not in the sinner's repentance. Rashi and Metzudat David add that God did not give this power to an angel, citing Exodus 23:21.
A Niphal: "be feared", "be held in awe". Metzudat Zion ties it to מורא, reverence. Ibn Ezra reads it as the effect of forgiveness on others: sinners hear of pardon and return.

verses.translation_literal: I wait for YHWH; my soul waits, and for his word I hope.
verses.translation_dramatic: I wait for the LORD. My whole self waits. And in his word, I put my hope.
verses.directors_commentary: Three verbs of waiting in one verse, and the Hebrew repeats the first root: קִוִּיתִי... קִוְּתָה, "I wait... waits". The KJV keeps the doubling but loses the point of the word. קוה originally means to stretch a cord taut (the noun קַו is a line), so the speaker is stretched toward God like a rope pulled tight; waiting here is tension, not idleness. The second verb, יחל, is a different word: Malbim distinguishes the two, calling קוה hope that rests in the soul even without a promise and יחל hope that stands on a given word. The text states exactly that: "for his word I hope". The soul (נֶפֶשׁ) is not an invisible inner part but the whole throat-and-breath person, the one who thirsts and gasps; the KJV's "my soul" is right if the reader hears it that way. Rashi hears the doubled waiting as a call to patience, like Psalm 27:14. Play the line low and steady after the shock of v. 3: this is the first calm in the psalm.

philological_notes.note: "I wait": the root means to stretch toward something, as a taut cord; hope as tension. Repeated with "my soul" as subject in the same verse. Rashi sees the repetition as waiting upon waiting, as in Psalm 27:14; Metzudat David says the doubling shows constancy.
"I hope": a Hiphil of יחל, used in the sense of the simple stem, as Meiri notes. Malbim contrasts it with קוה: this hope rests on a word that was given.

verses.translation_literal: My soul [waits] for my Lord, more than watchmen for the morning, watchmen for the morning.
verses.translation_dramatic: My soul waits for the Lord, more than the watchmen wait for morning — more than the watchmen, for the morning.
verses.directors_commentary: The image of the psalm. The watchman stands his post on the city wall through the dark hours, with no clock, only the sky; the morning means the end of the watch and the end of danger. The Hebrew has no verb in the first colon: "My soul — for my Lord". The KJV supplies "waiteth" and adds "I say" before the repetition; neither is in the Hebrew, and the second "I say" breaks the sound, because the Hebrew simply repeats, שֹׁמְרִים לַבֹּקֶר, like a second breath of the same waiting. The comparison is deliberate: the watchmen's hope is certain, but it is tied to a fixed hour, since dawn cannot come before the twelve hours of night have run (Malbim on v. 6). The soul's hope in God is greater because it is not bound to time; as Malbim says on v. 7, God can redeem before the appointed hour. Rashi hears the doubling as waiting that begins again, "an end after an end", watch after watch. Radak and Meiri record another old reading: the "watchers for the morning" are those who rise before dawn to pray. Direct the actor to hold the repetition, not to hurry it.

philological_notes.note: "Watchmen", "those who keep watch", the same root as "keep" in v. 3. Ibn Ezra takes them as the guards of the walls who comfort themselves that morning will come; Radak, Meiri and Metzudat Zion record the sense of those who wait or rise early.
The prefix מן here is comparative: "more than". The same preposition reads "from" in v. 1; the sense depends on the verb of longing that is missing.

verses.translation_literal: Hope, O Israel, to YHWH, for with YHWH is the covenant loyalty, and great with him is redemption.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hope, Israel! Hope in the LORD. For with the LORD there is steadfast love, and with him, redemption in abundance.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice turns from "I" to "you": the one speaker, alone in the depths, now speaks to the whole people. This is why the psalm sits among the pilgrim songs: a private cry becomes a call to the crowd on the road. "Hope" is the imperative of the same root as "I hope" in v. 5. The KJV's "mercy" is weaker than the Hebrew חֶסֶד, covenant loyalty: the faithfulness that holds to a bond after the other side has broken it. It is an obligation God has taken on himself, which is why the speaker can trust it. "Redemption" (פְּדוּת) is a market word: the price paid to buy back a slave, a captive, a firstborn or a mortgaged field. "Plenteous" in the KJV renders הַרְבֵּה, "abundance", set before its noun: "great with him is redemption". Radak and Metzudat David read the abundance as a record: God has redeemed Israel many times, so he does not run short of redemptions.

philological_notes.note: "The covenant loyalty", with the article: the loyal love that belongs to a bond. English "mercy" and "kindness" lose the sense of obligation. Radak: God's חסד is with all creatures always.
"Redemption", the buying back of a person or thing by paying a price; the noun is rare. Radak and Metzudat David read the abundance as God's record of many past redemptions.

verses.translation_literal: And he, he will redeem Israel from all his iniquities.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he himself will redeem Israel — out of all its wrongs.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm ends where it began, with iniquities, but the verb has changed: in v. 3 God could "keep" them; now he will buy Israel out of them. The sentence opens with an emphatic "he" (וְהוּא), "and he — he": the redeemer is God himself, no angel, no go-between, as v. 4 implied. The KJV's "redemption" in v. 7 and "redeem" here keep the Hebrew pairing of פְּדוּת and יִפְדֶּה, the market verb: a price, a release. And "from all his iniquities" is ambiguous in a useful way. עָוֺן means the wrong, its guilt and its penalty together, so Meiri can read "from the punishments that come because of the iniquities" (citing Gen 15:16 and Lam 4:22), while Radak reads the first step as forgiveness and the second as the return from exile. Metzudat David says the iniquity will not delay the redemption, because it has already been wiped away. The "his" refers to Israel, as a singular people: the psalmist who began alone has now spoken for everyone. End the reading quietly and let the last word hang.

philological_notes.note: "He will redeem": to ransom, to buy back. The same family as פְּדוּת in v. 7. Radak reads it as first forgiveness, then return from exile.
"His iniquities": the wrongs, and also what follows from them. Meiri cites Genesis 15:16 and Lamentations 4:22 for עון as punishment.
